`StaticSite` can serve straight from its bucket, `Router` can sign requests to Lambda function URLs, a Distributed Map can read and write its items in S3, and `sst dev` can give each stage its own AppSync Event API. `sst dev` also moves large messages faster, gets a streamed response through when AppSync loses a packet, and no longer drops a worker's first actions. Still built on upstream [v4.17.2](https://github.com/anomalyco/sst/releases/tag/v4.17.2).

Thanks to [@rogueturnip](https://github.com/rogueturnip), who sent six of the pull requests below and reported the problems behind them, and to [@jl4nz](https://github.com/jl4nz), who sent two.

### New

- **`sst.aws.StepFunctions.map` can read its items from S3, batch them, write its results to S3 and tolerate failed items.** `itemReader` reads the items from S3, either a `json`, `jsonl` or `csv` file or the list of `objects` in a bucket, `itemBatcher` hands them to each child execution in batches, `resultWriter` writes the results to a bucket under a `prefix`, and `toleratedFailurePercentage` and `toleratedFailureCount` let the Map finish when some items fail. So a distributed Map can process more than the 256 KB the state payload allows, and write large results. The state machine's role gets S3 permissions scoped to the bucket and to the key or prefix. There is a new example, `aws-step-functions-distributed-map`. ([#178](https://github.com/sst-community/sst/pull/178); [#171](https://github.com/sst-community/sst/issues/171), reported by [@AlperSakarya](https://github.com/AlperSakarya))
- **`sst.aws.StaticSite` can be served straight from its bucket,** with `edgeRouting: false`. The site then has no CloudFront Function and no KeyValueStore. That suits a single-page app, and an account whose policy, such as a service control policy that limits regions, denies the KeyValueStore API. `/` serves the `indexPage`, any other path serves the file at that exact path, and a missing file serves the `errorPage` with a 404, or the `indexPage` with a 200 when there is no `errorPage`. So `/about` no longer serves `about.html`, which the docs say. A request function is still created for an `edge.viewerRequest.injection`, or to block the CloudFront URL when there is a `domain`. It can't be combined with `router`. Existing sites don't change, and there is a new example, `aws-static-site-no-edge-routing`. ([#196](https://github.com/sst-community/sst/pull/196), by [@jl4nz](https://github.com/jl4nz))
- **`router.route()` can sign requests to a Lambda function URL.** Set `protection: true` on the route, as in `router.route("/api", fn.url, { protection: true })`, and the Router's `protection` (`"oac"` or `"oac-with-edge-signing"`) applies to it, so a function URL with IAM authorization works behind the Router instead of returning 403. It is off by default, so no existing route changes. The route has to point at a function URL (`<id>.lambda-url.<region>.on.aws`). `router.route()` only receives a URL, so you grant CloudFront the `lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl` and `lambda:InvokeFunction` permissions yourself, with `invokedViaFunctionUrl: true` on the second. With `"oac"`, POST, PUT and PATCH requests to an IAM-authorized function URL need an `x-amz-content-sha256` header, and the signature replaces the viewer's `Authorization` header. The docs have the details. ([#185](https://github.com/sst-community/sst/pull/185); [#184](https://github.com/sst-community/sst/issues/184), reported by [@hito-nm](https://github.com/hito-nm))
- **`sst dev` can give each stage its own AppSync Event API,** with `dev: { appsync: "stage" }` in the app config. By default every app and stage in an account and region shares one API, `sst`, and its per-API limit of 10,000 inbound events a second. With `"stage"`, `sst dev` finds the stage's API by its tags, or creates it, named `sst-<app>-<stage>`, and `sst remove` removes it with the stage. On a test with another developer sending about 10,000 events a second, two thirds of a request-heavy stage's requests failed on the shared API and the median took 14 seconds. On its own API the median didn't move, though its slowest requests (p99) took 4 to 10 seconds, and a few failed, because the account's own limits still apply. The function and task stubs' `appsync:*` permission reaches only that API. The default doesn't change. AWS allows 50 Event APIs per region by default, which is why this is opt-in, and `"stage"` needs a few more AppSync permissions, which the config docs and the IAM credentials page list. ([#187](https://github.com/sst-community/sst/pull/187), by [@rogueturnip](https://github.com/rogueturnip); [#174](https://github.com/sst-community/sst/issues/174), reported by [@rogueturnip](https://github.com/rogueturnip))

### Fixes

- **`sst dev` keeps watching files after the file watcher reports an error.** The watcher never read fsnotify's error channel, which is unbuffered, so the first error stopped every later file event until you restarted `sst dev`, and nothing said so. It logs the error and carries on. On Linux, a test that overflowed the inotify queue stopped the old watcher for good and the new one kept delivering events. ([#183](https://github.com/sst-community/sst/pull/183), by [@bunnysayzz](https://github.com/bunnysayzz); [#182](https://github.com/sst-community/sst/issues/182), reported by [@martijndierckx](https://github.com/martijndierckx))
- **Large function requests and responses move through `sst dev` faster.** A message over 128 KB went one packet at a time, a round trip each. Now it goes 5 packets to an AppSync request and up to 4 requests at once. A 6 MB reply went from a median of 6.2 seconds to 1.6 seconds, and a 1 MB request from 1.25 seconds to 0.72 seconds. A streamed response goes over HTTPS rather than the WebSocket, so up to 4 writes are in flight at once. The send timeout now scales with the size of a large request, which works down to an uplink of about 1.5 Mbit/s with 4 large requests at once. ([#191](https://github.com/sst-community/sst/pull/191), by [@rogueturnip](https://github.com/rogueturnip); [#173](https://github.com/sst-community/sst/issues/173))
- **`sst dev` gets a streamed function response through when AppSync loses a packet.** AppSync sometimes accepts a publish and never delivers it. A streamed response is sent once, so the bridge in your function waited for the missing packet until the function timed out and the caller got the stream cut short. The bridge now asks for the packets it is missing, and `sst dev` sends again the ones it kept (up to 32 MB, for 2 minutes). On a test through `sst dev`, 3 of 60 streams on the previous version waited the full 120 seconds and were cut short, and with this version all 60 arrived whole. It takes this version of the CLI and a bridge deployed by it: either alone changes nothing. ([#193](https://github.com/sst-community/sst/pull/193), by [@rogueturnip](https://github.com/rogueturnip); [#190](https://github.com/sst-community/sst/issues/190), reported by [@rogueturnip](https://github.com/rogueturnip))
- **`sst dev` no longer loses or misreports a worker's first actions.** A worker is recorded before it starts, so its first request for an invocation, its first invocation, its answer, its error and what it prints count as its own. Before, a worker that exited with an invocation queued, after asking before it was recorded, had the queue dropped and the caller waited until Lambda timed out. ([#195](https://github.com/sst-community/sst/pull/195), by [@rogueturnip](https://github.com/rogueturnip); [#194](https://github.com/sst-community/sst/issues/194), reported by [@rogueturnip](https://github.com/rogueturnip))
- **`sst dev` waits for a new AppSync Event API to accept connections.** A new Event API turns down its first WebSocket connect and its first subscribe for about a second, which made `sst dev` fail with `appsync connection failed`, or run without its subscription until the next reconnect. It now dials and subscribes again for up to 10 seconds, and closes each connection that was turned down. This applies to the shared API as well. ([#187](https://github.com/sst-community/sst/pull/187))

### Also

- The docs link the examples to this fork's repository ("View the full example", the start guides and the reference pages), so they reach examples the fork has ([#181](https://github.com/sst-community/sst/pull/181); [#180](https://github.com/sst-community/sst/issues/180), reported by [@AlperSakarya](https://github.com/AlperSakarya)).
- Some tests that failed now and then in CI are steadier ([#188](https://github.com/sst-community/sst/pull/188), [#192](https://github.com/sst-community/sst/pull/192), by [@rogueturnip](https://github.com/rogueturnip)).
- The repo's `document-component` agent skill has the frontmatter that agents need to find it ([#197](https://github.com/sst-community/sst/pull/197), by [@jl4nz](https://github.com/jl4nz)).

### Install

```bash
npm install sst@npm:@sst-community/sst@4.23.0
```

To switch an existing project:

1. Check that `node --version` shows `v22` or later, wherever you run `sst`, CI included.
2. Set its dependency to `"sst": "npm:@sst-community/sst@4.23.0"` and reinstall.

For a project that isn't JavaScript, install the CLI globally. It still needs Node.js 22 or later, to run `sst.config.ts`:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sst-community/sst/main/install | bash
```
